idiom_name: hand-written hub struct: per-event channel of {handler, user_data} pairs
implementation_notes: C supplies no in-process pub/sub at all, so the aggregator is a hand-written hub: one struct holds a growable array of subscriber entries ({void (*fn)(const event_t *, void *); void *ctx;}) per event type, subscribe appends an entry and publish walks a copy of that array, invoking each handler with the event pointer and its own context pointer. Both missing roles must be built by hand: the Subscriber becomes the function-pointer-plus-context pair (there are no objects to register) and the Channel becomes a table entry keyed by an event-type enum or string, with a queue or a mutex around it if publishers and consumers live on different threads. The classic hand-written form stays justified in embedded or dependency-averse code; where GLib is available its GObject signal system (g_signal_new/g_signal_connect/g_signal_emit with GCallback handlers and GDestroyNotify for the user data) is the library realization and removes most of the registry bookkeeping.
pitfalls: The context pointer is not owned by the hub: a subscriber that frees its own state without unsubscribing leaves a dangling void* that the next publish dereferences.
Iterating the live array while a handler subscribes or unsubscribes makes the hub read freed memory or skip entries - snapshot under the lock, then dispatch outside it.

There is no weak-reference story: unlike managed languages, a dead C subscriber is indistinguishable from a live one, so every module boundary needs an explicit unregister step in its teardown function.
Without a lock or a queue around the registry, a publish from an interrupt or another thread races the next subscribe.
